questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student has had a gradually worsening dry, non-productive cough, low-grade fever, and headache for 2 weeks but feels well enough to attend class. His chest X-ray is shown, with streaky, patchy interstitial infiltrates that look worse than his symptoms suggest. Which organism is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: M. pneumoniae is the leading cause of atypical ('walking') pneumonia in children and young adults: gradual onset, dry cough, mild symptoms, and patchy interstitial infiltrates that often look more severe than the patient appears. S. pneumoniae causes a lobar pneumonia with productive, rust-colored sputum; Legionella affects older or immunocompromised patients and usually gives a lobar pattern with high fever and diarrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae is the leading cause of atypical ('walking') pneumonia in children and young adults: gradual onset, dry cough, mild symptoms, and patchy interstitial infiltrates that often look more severe than the patient appears. S. pneumoniae causes a lobar pneumonia with productive, rust-colored sputum; Legionella affects older or immunocompromised patients and usually gives a lobar pattern with high fever and diarrhea.

questions.stem: A child develops the painful blistering skin rash and hemorrhagic erosions of the lips shown here two weeks after a respiratory infection with a dry cough. She took no new medications. Which pathogen is the most frequently identified infectious trigger of this condition?

explanation.summary: This is Stevens-Johnson syndrome: an immune-mediated reaction causing detachment of the epidermis and mucous membranes, with painful blisters and erosions of the lips, eyes, nose, and genitals. Medications are the most common cause overall, but M. pneumoniae is the most frequently identified infectious trigger, especially in children and adolescents.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is Stevens-Johnson syndrome: an immune-mediated reaction causing detachment of the epidermis and mucous membranes, with painful blisters and erosions of the lips, eyes, nose, and genitals. Medications are the most common cause overall, but M. pneumoniae is the most frequently identified infectious trigger, especially in children and adolescents.

questions.stem: A young adult recovering from a respiratory infection develops painful erosions of the lips and oral mucosa with crusting and involvement of the eye, as shown. Which condition is this?

explanation.summary: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is a serious immune-mediated disorder in which the epidermis and mucous membranes detach, producing painful blisters and erosions of the lips, eyes, nose, and genitals. It is triggered most often by medications; among infections, M. pneumoniae is the most common trigger. Its more severe form is toxic epidermal necrolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is a serious immune-mediated disorder in which the epidermis and mucous membranes detach, producing painful blisters and erosions of the lips, eyes, nose, and genitals. It is triggered most often by medications; among infections, M. pneumoniae is the most common trigger. Its more severe form is toxic epidermal necrolysis.

questions.stem: Colonies from a young adult with 'walking pneumonia' grow on a specialized medium supplemented with sterols and take on the 'fried egg' appearance shown. Which organism is this?

explanation.summary: M. pneumoniae has no cell wall and has sterols in its membrane, so it needs sterols in the medium and forms 'fried egg' colonies (mnemonic: 'eggs contain cholesterol'). Culture is slow and rarely done; PCR is the preferred diagnostic test.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae has no cell wall and has sterols in its membrane, so it needs sterols in the medium and forms 'fried egg' colonies (mnemonic: 'eggs contain cholesterol'). Culture is slow and rarely done; PCR is the preferred diagnostic test.

questions.stem: This electron micrograph shows a host cell whose cytoplasm is dominated by one large membrane-bound inclusion packed with small bacteria. These obligate intracellular bacteria survive and divide inside the host endosome mainly by doing what?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Resisting lysozyme with a thick peptidoglycan wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Preventing lysosome fusion with the endosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Escaping the endosome into the cytosol

explanation.summary: Chlamydia spp. are taken up into an endosome (the inclusionary body) and block lysosome fusion with it. They then make the endosome their home and divide rapidly until the inclusion fills most of the cell. They lack classic peptidoglycan, and the host cell lyses only after several rounds of division.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chlamydia spp. are taken up into an endosome (the inclusionary body) and block lysosome fusion with it. They then make the endosome their home and divide rapidly until the inclusion fills most of the cell. They lack classic peptidoglycan, and the host cell lyses only after several rounds of division.

questions.stem: Infected cells in culture are stained with iodine, showing the large brown intracytoplasmic inclusions seen here. Which organism forms these inclusions?

explanation.summary: Chlamydia spp. are obligate intracellular bacteria that replicate inside an endosome and form large inclusionary bodies. These inclusions can be stained with iodine, Giemsa, or immunofluorescent stains. Chlamydiae do not Gram stain, and in practice PCR (nucleic acid amplification) is the most common way to identify them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chlamydia spp. are obligate intracellular bacteria that replicate inside an endosome and form large inclusionary bodies. These inclusions can be stained with iodine, Giemsa, or immunofluorescent stains. Chlamydiae do not Gram stain, and in practice PCR (nucleic acid amplification) is the most common way to identify them.

questions.stem: This diagram shows a biphasic life cycle: a small infectious form enters a host cell, converts into a larger form that divides inside an endosome, converts back, and is released when the cell lyses. Which organism has this life cycle?

explanation.summary: Chlamydia alternates between elementary bodies (infectious, tough, spore-like particles that enter target cells) and reticulate bodies (non-infectious, metabolically active forms that replicate by binary fission inside the inclusionary body). Some reticulate bodies convert back to elementary bodies, which are released when the cell lyses and go on to infect neighboring cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chlamydia alternates between elementary bodies (infectious, tough, spore-like particles that enter target cells) and reticulate bodies (non-infectious, metabolically active forms that replicate by binary fission inside the inclusionary body). Some reticulate bodies convert back to elementary bodies, which are released when the cell lyses and go on to infect neighboring cells.

questions.stem: This scanning electron micrograph shows a Chlamydia-infected cell lysing at the end of the bacterium's developmental cycle. Which form of the organism is released to infect neighboring cells?

explanation.summary: After several rounds of division, some reticulate bodies convert back into elementary bodies. The infected cell then lyses and releases these infectious, spore-like elementary bodies, which attach to and enter neighboring cells. Reticulate bodies are non-infectious and replicate only inside the inclusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: After several rounds of division, some reticulate bodies convert back into elementary bodies. The infected cell then lyses and releases these infectious, spore-like elementary bodies, which attach to and enter neighboring cells. Reticulate bodies are non-infectious and replicate only inside the inclusion.

questions.stem: This electron micrograph shows a human phagocyte taking up a bacterium by wrapping it in concentric, spiraling layers of membrane. What is this distinctive uptake process called?

explanation.summary: Legionella pneumophila induces coiling phagocytosis when macrophages take it up. Inside the macrophage it prevents the phagosome from fusing with lysosomes, so it can persist and multiply.
explanation.whyCorrect: Legionella pneumophila induces coiling phagocytosis when macrophages take it up. Inside the macrophage it prevents the phagosome from fusing with lysosomes, so it can persist and multiply.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has a high fever, cough, watery diarrhea, and hyponatremia after a hotel stay. A sputum Gram stain shows neutrophils but few organisms. The fastidious organism, which requires iron and cysteine, grows on the medium shown. Which organism is it?

explanation.summary: L. pneumophila is a fastidious gram-negative rod that needs iron and cysteine and grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE, 'charcoal') agar. Legionnaires' disease often brings high fever, diarrhea, and hyponatremia, and is acquired from contaminated water sources. A urine antigen test (serotype 1) and PCR give rapid diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila is a fastidious gram-negative rod that needs iron and cysteine and grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE, 'charcoal') agar. Legionnaires' disease often brings high fever, diarrhea, and hyponatremia, and is acquired from contaminated water sources. A urine antigen test (serotype 1) and PCR give rapid diagnosis.

questions.stem: An elderly patient has severe pneumonia with high fever and diarrhea. The organism stained very poorly on Gram stain, so a silver stain of the sputum was done (shown), revealing dark rods. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: Legionella has a gram-negative structure but stains very poorly with the Gram stain; a silver stain can be used on sputum. Mycoplasma has no cell wall and Chlamydia is obligately intracellular, so neither shows up as rods free in sputum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Legionella has a gram-negative structure but stains very poorly with the Gram stain; a silver stain can be used on sputum. Mycoplasma has no cell wall and Chlamydia is obligately intracellular, so neither shows up as rods free in sputum.

questions.stem: The tick species shown here at its different life stages has mice as the reservoir of the pathogen it carries. The small, easily missed nymph is the usual culprit in spring and summer, and it must stay attached for 36-48 hours to transmit the bacterium. Which bacterium is it?

explanation.summary: The blacklegged (deer) tick, Ixodes scapularis, transmits B. burgdorferi, the cause of Lyme disease, from its mouse reservoir. Nymphs are small and go unnoticed, so they usually transmit the disease; adults are easily seen and removed. Removing the tick promptly, before 36-48 hours of attachment, rarely results in disease. R. rickettsii is carried mainly by Dermacentor ticks.
explanation.whyCorrect: The blacklegged (deer) tick, Ixodes scapularis, transmits B. burgdorferi, the cause of Lyme disease, from its mouse reservoir. Nymphs are small and go unnoticed, so they usually transmit the disease; adults are easily seen and removed. Removing the tick promptly, before 36-48 hours of attachment, rarely results in disease. R. rickettsii is carried mainly by Dermacentor ticks.

questions.stem: A hiker from the northeastern United States has fatigue, fever, and joint aches, along with the slowly expanding rash shown, which has a central clearing. Which organism causes this rash?

explanation.summary: Erythema migrans is a red rash that expands from the bite site and can take on a bull's-eye appearance. It is pathognomonic for early localized (stage 1) Lyme disease, caused by B. burgdorferi, but appears in only 70-80% of patients. The RMSF rash, by contrast, is maculopapular, starts on the wrists and ankles, and spreads to the trunk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erythema migrans is a red rash that expands from the bite site and can take on a bull's-eye appearance. It is pathognomonic for early localized (stage 1) Lyme disease, caused by B. burgdorferi, but appears in only 70-80% of patients. The RMSF rash, by contrast, is maculopapular, starts on the wrists and ankles, and spreads to the trunk.

questions.stem: Two patients with different skin tones each develop a single expanding red lesion at the site of a recent tick bite, along with fever, fatigue, and swollen lymph nodes. The lesions are shown. Which stage of disease do these findings represent?

explanation.summary: A single erythema migrans at the bite site, with fever, fatigue, and adenopathy, appearing days to a month after the bite, is stage 1 (early localized) Lyme disease. Stage 2 brings multiple rashes, meningitis, facial palsy, and heart block. Stage 3 brings chronic large-joint arthritis and neurologic symptoms. The rash can be hard to see on darker skin.
explanation.whyCorrect: A single erythema migrans at the bite site, with fever, fatigue, and adenopathy, appearing days to a month after the bite, is stage 1 (early localized) Lyme disease. questions.stem: In July, a patient from Arkansas has fever, severe headache, and myalgia. Two days later, the maculopapular rash shown appears on the wrists and ankles and spreads toward the trunk. He recalls a tick bite while hiking. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Rocky Mountain spotted fever, caused by R. rickettsii, presents with the triad of fever, headache, and rash. The maculopapular rash starts around the wrists, ankles, palms, and soles and spreads to the trunk, usually 2-4 days after the fever. R. rickettsii infects endothelial cells and causes widespread vasculitis. It is transmitted mainly by the American dog tick and is the most common fatal tick-borne disease in the U.S.

questions.stem: A park ranger has fever, headache, and myalgia 10 days after a tick bite, along with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. A peripheral smear shows the mulberry-shaped cluster of bacteria (arrow) inside a mononuclear phagocyte. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: Ehrlichia spp. are small, gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacteria with a tropism for monocytes and macrophages. Clusters of bacteria inside cell vacuoles form mulberry-like aggregates called morulae. These help distinguish ehrlichiosis from Lyme disease and RMSF, but they are not reliable enough for diagnosis on their own; serology usually confirms it. Ehrlichiosis is spread by the lone star tick and the blacklegged tick.
